title: How to Make Him Want You Back: Honest Steps That Work
h1: How to Make Him Want You Back: Honest Steps That Respect You Both
description: Wondering how to make him want you back? Learn honest, healthy steps: take space, work on yourself, understand what went wrong and reconnect the right way.
keyword: how to make him want you back
excerpt: A healthy, no-games approach to rekindling things with your ex: give it space, grow, understand what broke, and reach out the right way.
intro:
Maybe the breakup happened fast, or maybe it had been coming for a while. Either way, you can't stop thinking about him, and part of you believes there's still something worth saving. It's natural to want a second chance, and it's natural to search for the perfect move that will make him realize what he lost.

Here's the honest version: you can't control another person's feelings, and tricks like jealousy games or "playing dirty" tend to backfire or rebuild the same broken relationship. What you can do is become the healthiest, clearest version of yourself and create real conditions for reconnection. This guide shows you how to make him want you back without games, including how to tell whether getting back together is even a good idea.
body:
First, ask whether you really want him back

Before you plan anything, get honest with yourself. Breakups trigger a powerful urge to undo the loss, and that urge can feel identical to love. Ask yourself:

  • Do I miss him, or do I miss having someone?
  • Was the relationship mostly good, with a fixable problem, or was it mostly painful?
  • Did he treat me with respect and kindness?
  • If nothing changed, would I want this exact relationship again?

If the relationship involved control, cheating patterns, threats or cruelty, the kindest thing you can do for yourself is to move on rather than win him back. Our guide on how to know when your relationship is over can help you think it through.

Tip: If your ex was abusive or made you feel unsafe, please don't try to reconnect. The National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233, text START to 88788, thehotline.org) offers free, confidential support.

Give it space (and mean it)

The first and hardest step is to step back. A period of little or no contact, often a few weeks, does several things at once:

  • It lets the strong emotions from the breakup cool down on both sides.
  • It gives you clarity about what you actually want.
  • It gives him room to notice your absence on his own, without pressure.

This is not a manipulation tactic or a silent treatment. It's a pause for healing. If you share kids, a lease or work, keep contact brief, polite and practical.

What to avoid during this time

  • Late-night or tipsy texts and calls. They almost always come across as desperate or confusing.
  • Begging or bargaining. Pleading puts him in a position of power and erodes your self-respect.
  • Constant social media monitoring. Checking his profile keeps you stuck and anxious.
  • Vague, attention-seeking posts. Cryptic quotes about heartbreak rarely send the message you intend.

Understand what went wrong

If you get back together without understanding why you broke up, you'll likely end up in the same place. Reflect honestly:

  • What were the recurring arguments about?
  • Were there needs on either side that went unmet?
  • What was your part in the problems? (Not to blame yourself, but to see what's in your control.)
  • What was his part, and is it something he'd realistically be willing to change?

Write your answers down. You'll want this clarity if you do end up talking again.

It also helps to separate fixable problems from fundamental ones. Fixable problems include poor communication, too little quality time, or stress from a hard season like a move or a job change. Fundamental problems are deeper mismatches: one of you wants children and the other doesn't, you want different places to live, or trust was broken repeatedly. Fixable problems can be worked on with effort from both sides. Fundamental ones rarely disappear just because you miss each other.

Work on yourself, for yourself

Personal growth is the most attractive and the most useful thing you can do right now, and it pays off whether or not he comes back.

Take care of your body and mind

Sleep, eat well, move in ways you enjoy, and if you'd like, refresh your style. Not to put on a show for him, but because feeling good in your skin boosts your confidence and mood.

Rebuild your own life

Reconnect with friends, hobbies and goals that may have faded during the relationship. A full life makes you happier and shows, naturally, that you're doing okay.

Address your side of the problems

If you recognized patterns, like jealousy, poor communication or avoiding conflict, start working on them. A licensed therapist can be a big help here. Our guide on how to deal with jealousy may help if that was an issue.

Stay positive and kind in any contact

If you cross paths or need to talk, keep it warm and light. Be friendly, not intense. Show interest in his life without prying. Skip rehashing old fights. A relaxed, upbeat version of you reminds him of what he enjoyed about you, far more than a heavy conversation about the relationship ever could.

The same goes for mutual friends. Stay on good terms with people you both know because they matter to you, not to collect information or send messages through them.

Reach out the right way

Once some time has passed and you feel steady, you might decide to reconnect. Start small and low-pressure:

"Hey, I saw that band you love is touring again and thought of you. Hope you're doing well."

If he responds warmly, keep things light for a while. A friendly coffee or a casual catch-up is a good next step. If he doesn't respond, or responds coolly, respect that. Don't send follow-up after follow-up.

For more on what to say, see our post on texts to make him miss you.

Have the honest conversation

If things feel positive and you're both open to talking about trying again, be direct and mature:

  • Acknowledge what went wrong, including your part, without groveling.
  • Share what you've learned and what you'd do differently.
  • Ask what he'd want to be different too.
  • Agree on how you'd handle the old problems if they came back.

A second chance works best when both people are choosing it with clear eyes, not because one person wore the other down.

Pay attention to how he responds. Does he take some responsibility too, or does he place all the blame on you? Is he curious about rebuilding, or just enjoying the attention? A reunion where only one person is doing the work tends to slide back into the old patterns quickly. If you both want to try, couples counseling can give you a neutral space to work through what went wrong.

Tip: If you try again, consider going slowly at first: date each other rather than jumping straight back into the old routine. It gives you both a chance to see whether things have truly changed.

Tactics to skip (and why)

You'll find plenty of advice online that promises to make him come running. Most of it causes harm:

  • Making him jealous. It may get a reaction, but it builds a reunion on insecurity and mistrust.
  • Throwing parties to exclude him or "playing dirty." Games invite games back and make reconciliation harder.
  • Returning his things dramatically. Using belongings to send emotional messages often backfires.
  • Faking a total personality change. If you change, change for you. Pretending won't last.

If he doesn't want to get back together

Sometimes you do everything right and the answer is still no. That hurts, but it also gives you the clarity to heal fully. Let yourself grieve, lean on your friends, and keep investing in the life you've started building. Our guide on how to move on after a break up can help with the next chapter.

The bottom line

The healthiest answer to how to make him want you back is to stop chasing and start growing. Take space, understand what went wrong, become the happiest version of yourself, and reach out with honesty when you're ready. If he comes back, you'll be building something stronger. If he doesn't, you'll already be on your way to something better. Explore more breakup advice for support along the way.
takeaways: First decide whether the relationship was healthy enough to want back.
Give real space after the breakup to let emotions cool and gain clarity.
Understand what went wrong and work on your own side of it, for yourself.
Reconnect slowly with low-pressure, friendly contact and respect his response.
Skip jealousy games and manipulation; they rebuild the same broken relationship.

faq.q: How long should I wait before contacting my ex?
faq.a: Many people find a few weeks of little or no contact helpful, but there's no magic number. Wait until you feel calm, clear about what you want, and able to handle any response without spiraling. Reaching out from a steady place matters more than the exact timing.

faq.q: Does no contact make him miss you?
faq.a: Space can give him room to notice your absence, but it isn't a guaranteed tactic. Its real value is helping you heal and think clearly. Treat it as time for yourself rather than a strategy to control his feelings. Use the time to rebuild routines that make you feel like yourself again.

faq.q: Should I try to make my ex jealous?
faq.a: It's usually a bad idea. Jealousy might get a reaction, but it builds any reunion on insecurity and distrust and can push him further away. Honest, friendly contact and genuine personal growth are far more likely to lead somewhere healthy.

faq.q: How do I know if my ex wants me back?
faq.a: Signs include him reaching out on his own, asking about your life, suggesting plans to meet, or bringing up the relationship in a reflective way. Mixed signals aren't a clear yes. The surest way to know is an honest conversation.
